<reason>CON built a coherent route from its opening and held it: the motion justifies the ban by long-term cascades, low-altitude intercepts (2008, 2019) demonstrably did not create persistent debris, so "all" is overbroad, deletes the compliant low-shot path, and binds no one the Outer Space Treaty didn't already fail to bind. PRO's best moves were the self-grading/loophole worry and the "inspection after injection" framing, plus a fair pressure question that forced CON to concede neither rule compels Moscow or Beijing. But under CON's Q2 pressure PRO conceded 2008/2019 left no lasting catalogued harm and pivoted to a "collision lottery" of transient months-long risk, which CON convincingly showed abandons the motion's stated harm and would indict launches and deorbits equally. PRO's closing response ("those months are how a cascade begins") was asserted rather than shown, and the "violator has no reason to shoot low" point was left muddled. CON's clipped closing and a shaky claim that the 2009 collision outranked the 2007 test as the largest debris event are real but minor costs. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B3.2/B4 pressure sequence: CON asked PRO to name one lasting harm from the 2008 or 2019 intercepts; PRO's A2 answer that "lasting catalogued wreckage is the wrong test" conceded the point and shifted to transient collision risk, letting CON argue PRO's final speeches no longer defend the cascade harm the motion names.</best_rebuttal>
